clue.text: Work of features-writer, say

parts.note: a features-writer is jokingly someone who rewrites a person's facial features, as a cosmetic surgeon does

explanation.surface: A description of what a newspaper's features journalist produces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Features-writer' suggests journalism; here features are parts of the face, and the 'writer' who reworks them is a surgeon.
explanation.definitionFit: Cosmetic surgery that tightens the skin of the face is the work of someone who reshapes facial features.

clue.text: Delightful sort of day for a chortler?

definitions.text: Delightful sort of day for a chortler?

parts.words: Delightful sort of day for a chortler?
parts.note: points to the Jabberwocky line 'O ... day! Callooh! Callay!' as the father 'chortled in his joy'

explanation.surface: Asking what kind of day pleases someone who laughs a lot.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewis Carroll coined both this word and 'chortle' in the poem Jabberwocky.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonsense word by Lewis Carroll for joyous or wonderful, used of the day the monster was slain.

clue.text: Argument against writing for one who is pressed

parts.note: a con is an argument against, as in pros and cons
script means handwriting or a written text

explanation.surface: A case made against a writer under pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: To press someone into service, as a press gang did, is to force them to serve.
explanation.definitionFit: A person compulsorily enlisted into military service has been pressed, forced into the forces.

clue.text: Rich veins needed for long poems

parts.note: odes are lyrical poems

explanation.surface: Richly veined writing is required for lengthy poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: These are veins of metal ore in rock, rich deposits sought by miners.

clue.text: Turning-point for mechanics?

parts.note: a turning-point is reread literally: the pivot on which a lever turns, as studied in mechanics

explanation.surface: A decisive moment for garage workers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning-point' suggests a crisis and 'mechanics' car repairers; here mechanics is the branch of physics.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the pivot or support about which a lever turns, the point of rotation.

clue.text: Still a cause of interference

explanation.surface: Something motionless is blamed for disrupting a signal.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means motionless; as a noun it is the electrical crackle that disturbs radio reception.

clue.text: Eccentric patriot is one who works on the box, for example

definitions.text: one who works on the box, for example

indicators.note: eccentric means odd or off-centre, signalling the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An odd nationalist turns out to work in television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eccentric' rearranges PATRIOT IS. 'the box' suggests television; it is the box shrub, clipped into shapes.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who clips hedges and shrubs such as box into ornamental shapes is a hedge sculptor.

clue.text: Lifting the foot briefly

parts.note: taken as written
ft is the short form of foot

explanation.surface: Raising one's foot for a moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifting' suggests raising; it is slang for stealing.
explanation.definitionFit: To lift something is slang for stealing it, so lifting is stealing.

clue.text: Carefully examining cover for a banger

explanation.surface: Inspecting the skin of a sausage.
explanation.walkthrough: A banger is British slang for a sausage; criminals 'case' a place they plan to burgle.
explanation.definitionFit: To case a place is to inspect it closely before a crime; a sausage skin is also called this.

clue.text: First signs of synovitis — knee eased with embrocation, rubbing and pin through joint

indicators.note: the first letter of each of the following words is taken in turn

explanation.surface: Medical notes on treating an inflamed knee with liniment, massage, and a surgical pin.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as orthopaedics, but 'joint' is a joint of meat.
explanation.definitionFit: A long metal or wooden spike pushed through a joint of meat to hold it while roasting.

clue.text: A women's leader Edward bearded

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter, so the first letter of women's is taken

parts.note: Ned is a familiar short form of the name Edward

explanation.surface: A man called Edward leads the women and wears a beard.
explanation.walkthrough: In botany a bearded grass or grain head has bristles, called awns.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanically, having bristly awns on the grain head is described as bearded, as with barley.

clue.text: But they were not mere rhymesters!

definitions.text: But they were not mere rhymesters!

parts.words: But they were not mere rhymesters!
parts.note: 'mere' is a lake, so the poets named are, punningly, not 'mere' writers but writers of the lakes

explanation.surface: An exclamation defending some writers as more than versifiers.
explanation.walkthrough: A mere is a lake; Wordsworth, Coleridge and Southey lived in England's Lake District and were known by its name.
explanation.definitionFit: Wordsworth, Coleridge and Southey were a group of Romantic writers named after the Lake District where they lived.

clue.text: Spill trifle on white bowl?

indicators.note: in an across clue one piece set on another follows it, so the trifle comes after the bowl

parts.note: in the game of bowls the jack is the small white ball aimed at
a straw is something worthless, a trifle

explanation.surface: Someone knocks a pudding over onto a white serving dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spill' looks like a verb about the trifle; it is a noun, a thin stick used in the game of spillikins.
explanation.definitionFit: In the game of spillikins each thin stick is a spill, also called by this name.

clue.text: Continue to play in London district

indicators.note: one piece added to another, so the word for continue is attached after the word for play

parts.note: to act is to play a part
on, as in 'carry on', means continue

explanation.surface: Instructions to keep performing somewhere in London.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a district of west London, in the borough of Ealing.

clue.text: Unvarying habit

explanation.surface: A routine that never changes.
explanation.definitionFit: Unvarying means the same throughout; a habit is a distinctive dress such as a nun's, like official dress worn by a group.

clue.text: Bad heart, not completely sound

parts.note: food that has gone off has gone bad
the heart of something is its centre

explanation.surface: A weak heart means less than perfect health.
explanation.definitionFit: Something slightly askew or a little odd is not quite right, not entirely sound.

clue.text: Promoting docked muscatel, for example

indicators.note: a docked tail is cut short, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: raising someone means promoting them

explanation.surface: Advertising a cut-price dessert wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'docked' removes the final G. Muscatel is both a wine and a dried grape from muscat vines.
explanation.definitionFit: Muscatel is a kind of dried grape made from the muscat variety.

clue.text: Intolerant of the continental Braille characters

parts.note: il is the word for 'the' in Italian, a continental language

indicators.note: the letters, or characters, of the word are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone narrow-minded about European Braille lettering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters' rearranges BRAILLE into LIBERAL. 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Narrow-minded and opposed to freedom of opinion, the opposite of broad-minded.

clue.text: Stoke Poges, say, a district of comparatively high unemployment

definitions.text: a district of comparatively high unemployment

explanation.surface: A Buckinghamshire village described as a jobless black spot.
explanation.walkthrough: Stoke Poges is where Thomas Gray wrote his Elegy in a Country Churchyard, so it is punningly 'Gray area'; 'say' signals the spelling is near enough.
explanation.definitionFit: Wordplay on the poet Gray's home ground; in British planning, a region of fairly high joblessness that missed full development aid.

clue.text: Cover up part of Nijinsky's leg?

explanation.surface: Hiding part of the famous dancer's leg.
explanation.walkthrough: Nijinsky is the dancer but also a famous racehorse, 1970 Triple Crown winner; a horse's leg has a joint called the stifle.
explanation.definitionFit: To suppress or smother something is to cover it up; in a horse the joint above the hock on the hind leg has this name.

clue.text: Spotted quarters marked with two colours

parts.note: E and S are two compass points, or quarters
pied means patched in two colours, like a magpie

explanation.surface: Piebald areas noticed on a coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' suggests markings; it is the past tense of see.
explanation.definitionFit: To spot something is to catch sight of it, the old word being to espy.

clue.text: Long-time-no-see, this sort of bishop?

parts.note: the greeting 'long time no see' is reread as a see, a bishop's diocese, that has long ceased to exist

explanation.surface: A greeting after a long absence, applied to some kind of bishop.
explanation.walkthrough: A see is a bishop's diocese; a bishop given the title of an extinct see has a see that no one has seen for a long time.
explanation.definitionFit: A bishop holding the title of a defunct see, with no actual diocese, is described as one in name only.

clue.text: Harness horse with a pig's foot?

explanation.surface: A horse in harness with a hoof like a pig's.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse bred for trotting races in harness; a pig's foot cooked as food has the same name.

clue.text: Not far from resort of St Malo

indicators.note: resort is read as re-sort, so the letters of the words are sorted anew

explanation.surface: Somewhere near a French seaside town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resort of' looks like a holiday town; read as re-sort, it rearranges ST MALO.
explanation.definitionFit: Nearly, as in 'nearly there', is close to but not quite, near the mark.

clue.text: Desert holiday

explanation.surface: A break spent in the desert.
explanation.definitionFit: To desert is to go away and abandon; leave is also time off granted from work or the army.

clue.text: A university study of American poet

parts.note: a den is a private study or workroom

explanation.surface: An academic paper on a poet from the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: W. H. Auden was English-born but took US citizenship in 1946.
explanation.definitionFit: W. H. Auden, born in York, became a United States citizen and wrote much of his later verse there.

clue.text: Does he have the smaller share at lunchtime?

definitions.text: Does he have the smaller share at lunchtime?

parts.words: Does he have the smaller share at lunchtime?
parts.note: a share is also the blade of a plough, and the lad at the plough is junior to the man who gives the ploughman's lunch its name

explanation.surface: A question about who gets less food at lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: A ploughshare is a plough's cutting blade; a ploughman's lunch is a British pub meal of bread, cheese and pickle, and the boy would get a smaller portion than the man.
explanation.definitionFit: A youth who leads or guides the horses pulling a plough on a farm.

clue.text: Storms announced for Scottish Highlanders

indicators.note: announced means spoken out, so the word sounds like the one said

parts.note: gales are violent winds or storms

explanation.surface: Bad weather forecast for the north of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Celtic people of the Highlands, Gaelic speakers, are known by this ethnic name.

clue.text: London tube station changes deter lots

indicators.note: the letters of the following words are changed into a new order

explanation.surface: Changing trains at a London Underground station causes many delays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changes' rearranges DETER LOTS. 'Changes' fits a tube station so well it hides its role.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a stop on the Northern line of the London Underground, near Shoreditch.

clue.text: Headless monster is a delusion

indicators.note: without a head, so the word loses its opening letter

parts.note: a terror is a frightful creature or monster

explanation.surface: A headless monster is only an illusion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Headless' removes the initial T.
explanation.definitionFit: A mistaken belief is a delusion, a sense of the word as a misconception.

clue.text: Romantic proposal

explanation.surface: A loving offer, perhaps of marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: Romantic means loving and gentle; a formal offer, as in a bid for a contract, is also so called.

clue.text: Obedient wife chosen from Greek ladies, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the letters of ladies might be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: A dutiful wife selected from among Greek women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges LADIES into ISELDA. 'chosen from' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Patient Griselda, from Boccaccio and Chaucer, is the legendary model of a wife who submits to every trial.
